The Defence counsel of the accused, who are to your left, there are many of them, as you can see, but only one per accused will have the right to ask questions of you, and they will also have the same amount of time, that is an hour and a half. In view of the time envisaged, if the Defence uses all the time, it will be necessary for you to come back tomorrow morning to continue your testimony if we don't complete it today. So I would like to ask you to answer questions put to you with precision. The four Judges in front of you may also ask you questions, and they certainly will do so. And we Judges also request very precise answers from you. The questions will relate to who, how, when. That will be the kind of questions we will be asking you in connection with the events you will be telling us about. So we'll have some follow-up questions to others put to you. If you don't understand a question, don't hesitate to ask that it be reworded. And without further ado, I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a point of clarification to commence. The Prosecution has previously notified that this witness is to be called by us pursuant Rule 92 ter, and I believe the Chamber should be in possession of that information as well as the Defence having been notified of that. That will obviously affect some of the timings that Your Honour has outlined, and I can assist certainly as far as the Prosecution are concerned. We should -- I should not be longer than about 25 to 30 minutes with this witness. As is the normal practice, Your Honour, I will first read out the brief summary of the witness's statement before turning to the appropriate questions for tendering of that statement. The witness is a Muslim woman from Uzricje. Uzricje had a mixed population of Muslims and Croats. There were approximately 100 houses. Until January 1993, there were no real problems. During the night of the 12th and 13th of January, 1993, the Croats started shelling the village. The witness and about 50 Muslim villagers took shelter in a dugout. At about 5.00 a.m., the Croats entered Uzricje and ordered the Muslims to surrender and to walk to the centre of the village. The witness saw Ustashas entering the Muslim houses, looting them and then setting them on fire. The Muslims were divided up into two groups of 20 and put into two houses which were both guarded by the Ustashas. The witness and other detainees remained in the houses for 45 days and lived on the food that was stored there. After about five days, Ustashas took out the Muslim men and beat them up in order to get information --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I'm going to object. This -- for a witness to occasionally use the word Ustasha may be inevitable, but for counsel to use it while giving a precise of the statement is really inexcusable and I ask the counsel be asked to apologise and correct the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can respond to that. The very reason I'm using the word is, as counsel for the Defence may well notice, is that the witness almost exclusively uses this term herself in her statement, and for fear of substituting it with another word and getting objections with regard to that, I did not substitute my own vocabulary for that which is used by the witness in her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Gillett. You should have said at the outset that the witness uses this term in her statement but that you would use the Croatian word that is used in the indictment. But now we will see for ourselves whether the witness actually used this term. But as you are providing us with a summary now, you're providing a summary of the statement for the Judges, and you can say that she used this term, but don't use the term "Ustasha" all the time. We'll be wasting time otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness uses two terms in the statement, the HVO and the Ustasha. It depends on the situation, on the description. We can't say what criteria are involved, so it's not true to say that this is the term that she uses consistently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll see about that as things unfold. Please continue, Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be clear, might I continue and substitute the word for Croats?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. After about five days, Croats took out the Muslim men and beat them up in order to get information about weapons and front lines. The witness's sister-in-law was robbed of her gold rings by a Croat. On 13th of February, 1993, everyone was lined up outside against a wall by the Croats and interrogated about the killing of an HVO soldier. Croats threatened to kill all the detainees, and they were made to stand outside in the winter cold for the whole day. Some of the men were also beaten up. In early March, 1993, the witness and some relatives managed to escape the house and flee to Bugojno. That is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, if I can turn -- ask you some questions now concerning your statement, and firstly, whether you remember being interviewed by somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall on what date that was?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I think it was in January. I -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall the year?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And at the time when you were being interviewed, did you answer the questions put to you truthfully?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you do so voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: At the end of the interview, do you recall that the statement was read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall at that time signing a written statement that had been prepared to confirm that it was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, I see you have the statements that have already been placed in front of you, and I'd like to ask you whether you've had the opportunity of re-reading your statement prior to coming into court today.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you read your statement yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if you look on each of the pages, I believe in the English version, are those your initials or signature on each of the pages?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, if I were to ask you questions today about the subject matters contained in that statement, are your answers reflected in that witness statement?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, having had the opportunity of re-reading the statement in your own language, do you have any corrections or additions or indeed withdrawals that you'd like to make of that statement?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I stand by this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, turning more to the contents of that statement, a point of clarification. In paragraph 8 of both the English and the B/C/S versions of that statement, you mention that on the 30th of April, 1992, you had gone to visit your sister. Could you clarify where your sister lives?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, my sister and I live in Donji Vakuf. I lived there before the war. My sister lives in Gornji Vakuf. I went to see her since the Serbs issued an ultimatum to the Muslims in Donji Vakuf and said that they should leave Donji Vakuf. So I went to stay there with my sister. I stayed there as a refugee up until 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, did your sister -- is that in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf that she lives or in the town of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: In the town of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: At the time back in April of 1992, did you have any reason to go to Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: In April, 1992, she was in Uzricje. We were up there, and we lived there up until 1993, until the beginning of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, another point of clarification. Throughout your statement, it can be seen that you refer to Ustasha. What do you mean by this term "Ustasha," or who do you mean by this term "Ustasha"?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: When we were captured, when we were in the dugout, these soldiers who came to fetch us, well, they said, "The Ustashas have come to get you." "Let's hoist the white flag as if we were to surrender." But I don't make any distinctions. That's how they presented themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, do you remember what these people who you've referred to as Ustasha were wearing?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, some of them were wearing camouflage uniforms, and their faces were painted. Others were in black uniforms, and they -- they had also painted their faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any badges on either the black or the camouflage clothing?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I didn't see badges of any kind. They had some sort of ribbons on them, that's all. Black and red ribbons. But I didn't see any other kind of insignia on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you also mention in your statement somebody by the name of Pero Zulj, and you say in your statement that he was an HVO soldier. How do you know that he was an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Because when they drove us out of the houses at about 9.00 in the morning, they then asked us whether we knew who had killed Pero Zulj. He was an HVO member. There were only women and children in the houses. We didn't have weapons or anything. So I found out from them that he was an HVO member.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, again you also mention, this time in paragraph 16 of both the English and the B/C/S version of the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Madam, as far as you can remember, can you tell us the exact sentence that you heard in relation to the HVO soldier who was killed? What did they say exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They arrived in the morning and they drove us out of the house. We stood outside from 9.00 in the morning until 4.00 in the afternoon. It was cold. They fired shots. They said that they would kill the men and that they would shut us in the house and burn it down. The children were crying. They asked who had killed Pero Zulj, an HVO member. We didn't know who Pero Zulj was. We were quite simply refugees there. We didn't even know the inhabitants very well. All we wanted to do was to save our children and ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll stop you there. You said that they spoke about Pero Zulj. They mentioned Pero Zulj, but what was the exact term that they used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mention, Witness, at paragraph 16 of both the English and the B/C/S versions of the statement that an HVO soldier from the same village named Ivo intervened and told the Ustashas that they would have to kill him first and then the Muslims. Now, what I wanted to ask you again is how did you know that Ivo was an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, because Ivo had a camouflage uniform on him, and he had HVO insignia on his sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know this man Ivo? Do you know his full name?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know the names of the inhabitants who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, again in your statement you see his name -- or the name Ivo comes up again in paragraph 12. Can you clarify whether the Ivo you mention in paragraph 12 of your statement is also the same Ivo that is mentioned in paragraph 16 or whether these are different Ivos?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes, they are the same?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Still in paragraph 12 of your statement, you mention that your house was on fire and that you also saw Ustasha entering Muslim houses, looting and setting them on fire. Are you able to say how many houses were set on fire in Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, all the Muslim houses were set on fire with the exception of three or, rather, there was the house -- two houses we were accommodated in, and another house in which an old man lived who was bedridden, but all the other houses that were set on fire were Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And again still talking about this same incident, you say you saw these Ustasha entering the Muslim houses. What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, they were wearing black uniforms and camouflage uniforms, and their faces had been painted a certain colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Again, did you notice any badges on either the black or the camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, finally, I'd like you to turn to that bundle that you're holding in front of you to the other document that is there which is Exhibit 7350. And you'll see there's an English language version as well as the B/C/S version. If you turn to the B/C/S version, and you will see that this document is making reference to events in the village of Uzricje and about a conflict between the ABiH and the HVO in Gornji Vakuf on the 11th of January, 1993, until May, 1993, and it talks of looting and burning everything that was Muslim in the village of Uzricje. Does that accord with your experience in the village of Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I don't know these names, yes, but everything was looted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness. It only leaves me to tender the witness's statement and the document that I have just shown the witness. The Exhibit number of the statement is 9711, and the exhibit number that I just mentioned for the document is 7350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam, I have a question I'd like to put to you. It concerns when looting started in your village. In your written statement, in paragraph 11, you say that it was in the night of the 12th and 13th of January that the looting commenced. Do you have a perfect recollection of this night? I assume you were sleeping. What woke you up? Can you tell us what you can remember? Can you tell us how all of this started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They started shelling the village, and there were a number of Muslim houses in the middle of the village and there was a dugout there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say "they." That could mean anyone. It could be the ABiH. It could be UNPROFOR. We don't know. You say "they." Who shelled the village? Can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croats shelled the village. We took shelter in the dugout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say the Croats. Why do you say that the Croats did this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was no one else. I don't know how to explain this. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say there was no one else. The Croats who shelled the village, and you say that this happened in the night of the 12th and 13th. On the 12th, were you aware of the fact that there were HVO members in the vicinity of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because we were in the dugout, and it was only in the morning when they came to fetch us and when they wanted to take us out. We'd been shelled throughout the night. We were told to show a white flag because Ustashas had come to pick us up. That's how they presented themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you can remember, when did the looting of your village start exactly, on which date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 11th, the 12th, and the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before the 11th, nothing happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there ABiH or Territorial Defence members in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And outside the village, were there any ABiH soldiers protecting the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever leave the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Because we were in the dugout. We didn't leave the dugout to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But what I want to know is the following: Prior to the 11th of January, did you ever leave the village, and did you see either members of the HVO or of the ABiH outside the village, maybe a hundred metres away from the periphery of the village or a kilometre away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I never left. I was a refugee, and it wasn't necessary for me to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when one lives in a village, one usually leaves the village. One moves around. But you stayed within the limits of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I stayed in the village. It wasn't necessary to go anywhere. The children were quite young.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was this village protected by the ABiH or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, because there was a Croatian village in front of the village, exclusively a Croatian village, whereas in Uzricje the population was mixed. There was Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, the village next to your village, next door, what is the name of this village inhabited by Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I think it's Paloc, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How far away was this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was right next to the town. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that there was looting and you were in the dugout. Were you there to protect yourselves, to take shelter given the shelling of the houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your written statement, you say that there were about 50 of you in the dugout. Is that the correct number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you surrendered, when you got out, was there someone who had a white flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Someone did have a white flag, but I can't remember who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 50 individuals who were with you, they were women, children, and adults, I assume. Were there any inhabitants of the village or ABiH soldiers who were with you, who were among this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no soldiers. There were refugees, and there were families. There were the Kurbegovics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were no ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence has an hour and a half, so that should be a sufficient amount of time for this witness. The first Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before cross-examination begins, I would like to interpose an objection to the tendering of the Exhibit P 7350. The witness said, this is at page 62, line 22 of the transcript, that she did not know any of the names in this document. It's clear that she cannot identify any of the people referred to. It's not her document. And, Your Honour, this is not a document she can in any way authenticate. So on the basis of the Trial Chamber's decision on evidence of 13th of July, 2006, I object to the tendering of the document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll rule on that. Can we have the first Defence team, please. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ma'am. I'm counsel Tomasegovic Tomic from Zagreb and I will be questioning you on behalf of the fifth accused. Can you tell me, please, madam, in answer to a question from the Prosecution, you said that before visiting your sister that the Serbs had issued an ultimatum to the Muslims. In paragraph 8, it says the ultimatum was addressed to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: This may be a mistake in the translation, because there were only 3 per cent Croats in Donji Vakuf before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So the ultimatum was to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only to the Muslims. This must be a mistake in the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel approach the microphone, please. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, madam, when clarifying the point regarding Ustashas, you said that you called those persons Ustashas because when they came in front of the dugout and asked you to surrender with the white sheet they called themselves Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is how they introduced themselves, and we left the dugout.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You mention Ustashas several times in your statement in connection with the other events. So in paragraph 12 you say that you saw Ustashas looting and torching, then Ustashas took down -- your ID. Then the Ustashas separated you into two groups. Then in the same paragraph: Ustashas guarded in front of the house. Then in paragraph 14: Ustashas took out some men and beat them up. So there are more such references. I would like to know whether in each of these cases did the persons say that they were Ustashas, or was this the same group who said that they were Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I didn't know any of them. They always referred to themselves as being Ustashas. They would say that they were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Were they one and the same people?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't. I don't really know. Some were painted -- they had their faces painted. Some were taller, some were shorter but they kept saying they were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I see. So there were several groups of them?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, madam, before these events in January, 1993, the houses in Uzricje, how were they heated? Did they have central heating or wooden stoves?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Wooden stoves. All the houses had such stoves.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. After the events in January when you ended up in the dugout, could you tell me, please, was there any electricity in the village?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: There was no electricity at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: In the whole village?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: In the whole village.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have two more questions for you only. Tell me, please, after seeking shelter in the dugout when the shelling started, until the surrender with the white sheet you didn't leave the dugout?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So you couldn't see what was going on outside the dugout?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No, only when we left the left the dugout.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: But this was when you had surrendered?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: There's a technical point I'd like to clear up in your statement. You said that when the Ustasha came in front of the dugout - that is paragraph 11, can you find it for me, please - that they told you to come out with a white sheet as a sign of surrender. As you didn't have a white sheet, "One of us went to a nearby house and brought it."

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: They took out a woman. I don't remember whether it was a man or a woman, but they took this person to the next-door house to find a white sheet. So they took this person to find a white sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I see. So they took out one of you to find the sheet?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question. In paragraph 17, you describe an event in Bugojno. You say that you were put up in a vacant house that belonged to Croats.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: But that is what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, in Bugojno, when we got to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Tell me, please, who put you up in this house?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: The locals who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And where were the Croat owners of the house?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: No authority put you up there?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So a neighbour on his own initiative put you up in someone else's house?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam. In your statement -- I see you have it in front of you, so please look at it. In paragraph 12, at the very bottom of the Croatian version, the sentence reads: "While we were standing in the centre, an Ustasha took Tahir and a man called Softa towards the dugout and then Tahir's father-in-law came up to us and made inquiries about Tahir. We told him that a Ustasha had taken him to the dugout. Tahir's father-in-law then asked his neighbour, a Croat Ivo, whose surname I don't know, to go to the dugout and find out what had happened to Tahir and Softa. Ivo learnt that both of them had been killed and their dead bodies were found near the dugout. Tahir's father-in-law then buried both of them in the same grave." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did the event occur exactly in the way you described it?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Maybe after three or four or five days they were buried. They wouldn't let them walk around until then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It follows from this that you didn't see them being killed.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them being killed. I just saw them being taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This man called Tahir Plivcic, is he a local?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No. He was also a refugee from Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And this other person whom you call Softa, he was a local?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: He was a local.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, a moment ago in answer to a question, you said that there were no TO or BH army members in the village, is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did anyone have any weapon in the village? Did anyone open fire towards the Croats while you were in the village?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons on the people who were taken away from the village?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't see anyone because we were in the dugout.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tahir Plivcic or the man you refer to as Softa, did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Tahir didn't, but later I learnt that they had found something in Softa's place and not in Tahir's.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But where was Tahir living?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I suppose he was living in his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So Tahir was living in Softa's house, and in that house a sniper was found?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I heard that apparently it was found.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was the sniper the reason that they were taken away from there?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, you're just saying that a sniper was found there. How did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I will show the witness. I didn't intend to do that, but I will continue this line of questioning, and I'll show her where I get this information from, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you, on the 10th of February, 1994, give a statement to the security sector in Zenica, a statement about the events that took place in Uzricje? This is not the statement you have in front of you. Did you make a statement on the 10th of February, 1994, in Bugojno, in the SUP as we called it then, a statement about the events that took place on the 13th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I don't know that I did in Bugojno. I did make a statement, but I don't know whether it was in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't wish to tender this statement into evidence, but as I will have some questions for the witness linked to this statement, I wish to point out that it is a statement disclosed to us by the Prosecution. It has an ERN number, and I'd like to ask the usher to put the statement on the ELMO so that the witness can verify her signature, and I'd like the first page of this statement to remain under the overhead projector. Before you look at this statement, could you please pay attention first to what I'm going to say. When in paragraph 16 of the statement in front of you spoke about the event when you were taken out and asked about Petar -- Pero Zulj, can you remember whether the soldiers told you that one HVO member was killed or two?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: One, Pero Zulj.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did they perhaps tell you that two HVO members had been looted and killed?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No. They only mentioned Pero Zulj.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Will you now look at the statement that you have under the ELMO to your right. You can look through it, look at the page 2 and see your signature to confirm whether this is your signature.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Look at page 1 and remind yourself of what you said then. Page 1, please. Can we see page 1 on the ELMO, please. Page 1 on the ELMO. Thank you. The paragraph beginning with "About 12.00." I will read your description of this event. And here you remembered the person called Jusuf Softic. Was this the same Softa you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say here: "About 12.00 --" are you following me? "About 12.00 on the 18th of January, 1993, the Ustashas took from Softic Jusuf's garage his car and pushed it into the Trnovaca river in Uzricje. This was done by a Ustasha whom they called Babo, together with a couple of other Ustashas. Jusuf asked them what they were doing, and Babo just asked him where his house was. Jusuf pointed out his house immediately. The Ustashas entered his house. They stayed there for a while, and then they came back carrying a sniper rifle. Since Tahir Plavcic was standing next to Jusuf, they asked him where he lived, and when Tahir said that he was a refugee from Donji Vakuf and that he was living in Jusuf's house, Babo ordered them to go with him. As soon as they moved away a little, he opened fire at them. He killed Jusuf Softic immediately, while Tahir Plivcic lived for another three or four hours. But they wouldn't let anyone give him aid." Did you say this to the person asking for your statement?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, because Ivo told us this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What did Ivo tell you, that a sniper rifle was found?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that the sniper rifle was found and that they took them away and -- and this Babo killed this one person and wounded the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But in this statement, madam, you say as if you knew this, as if this is your own statement.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: It may appear to be that, but I didn't see this. But this was what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the statement in front of you, in paragraph 12, you said that Tahir's father-in-law asked his Croat neighbour Ivo, whose surname you don't know, to go to the dugout and to find out what happened to Tahir and Softa, and that he found out that both had been killed and that their bodies had been found next to the dugout. From what you told the Prosecutor, it would emerge that Ivo came at Tahir's request to look for these two persons. How is it possible, then, that Ivo knew about the sniper and everything else?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably told him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: How do I know who?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you didn't see the sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I did not, but Ivo said that a sniper rifle had been found.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell the investigator this when you made this statement? Why did you leave this out?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you asked what Ivo found out and what had happened to Tahir and Softa? Did anyone ask you about that when you were making your statement?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at this statement further. Let me ask you who told you this. At the bottom of the page -- can we move the page up, please, to the bottom so we can see the last few lines of the statement. So look at this. And you say -- what you've said in 1994, when your recollection of the event must have been better than it is today, 12 years later -- you made the statement in 1994. Did you remember the events better then than you do today? Are you hearing me? Don't read it. I will read it to you. I'm asking you a question. Did you remember the events better in 1994 than you do today?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, I do remember, but it all depends. These memories come back, and it's all mixed up in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at what you said in 1994 about this event. I'm reading -- I'm reading the last paragraph. "On 13th of February, 1993, at about 9.00, the Ustashas drove out all civilian Muslims from Uzricje and lined us up in front of Omer Filipovic's house. They requested that we tell them who looted and killed two HVO members from Rame." Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So what is right? In the statement today, you said that they only asked about the killing of Pero Zulj. When I asked you explicitly whether two persons were mentioned, you said they weren't. When I asked you whether they asked who had looted these people you said no. Did they ask you about two or one HVO member? Did they say that the killed persons were also looted?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Asked us about two. Pero Zulj is someone else. I'm afraid I don't understand the question at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The question is very clear. Before showing you this statement, which you have probably forgotten, I asked you whether on the day that you referred to in paragraph 16, that is the 13th of February, 1993, when they drove you out of the houses, did they ask you about one person? Did they ask you about Pero Zulj? Or did they ask you about who killed another HVO member in addition to Pero Zulj? Your answer was they only asked about Pero Zulj. Now you're telling me that they asked about another person. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Madam, do you see the difference?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do see the difference. I know that -- that we were forced out to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You never mentioned execution until now. You see how lightly you use words.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: A moment ago you said Ustasha, that they themselves called them that. You never said in this statement that they called themselves Ustashas. Not only the persons who told you to come out of the dugout, but you said that everyone who was there said that they were Ustashas. Well, how are we going to believe what you're saying? Did they ask you about one HVO member or two HVO members? Please make up your mind. What is it? What is the truth?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I know that they asked us about Pero and these people from Rama.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From Rama. These people from Rama. That means a number of them were killed?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: We were in the house. We'd been locked up in there. We didn't know who was passing through. There were blankets over the windows.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have to go back to something. Did they ask about one HVO member who had been killed or about a number of HVO members? Could you answer that question briefly so that we can move on? I don't want to bother you too much with this issue. You're probably aware of this. Please, I don't want to waste any time. I'd just like to inform the Court that I have received some time from Mr. Praljak's Defence, but I'll conclude my cross-examination very quickly.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: They asked about Pero Zulj.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did they ask you about other HVO members? Other HVO members who had been killed and looted? Did they ask about other HVO members who had been killed and looted?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. And now I'd like to go back to your departure. In item 17 in your statement, you mention the time that you left the house. You left with your sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How old was your sister-in-law at the time?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, she was born in 1935.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: About 60 or 65; I'm not very good at calculations.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Nor am I.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So your sister-in-law was with you and two children. Were these small children?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, my sister-in-law and her two-month old child. And my children were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So there was your sister-in-law and her child and how many children did you have?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Two. My sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So there were these women and two children. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How did you leave? That was -- there were four women, three children. So how did you leave the house?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no one there. They used that route to go to Croatia. That was the main route. They probably thought we were inhabitants, local inhabitants. It was 5.00 in the morning. There was no one there. We left before dawn broke. We didn't even meet anyone on the way. We didn't see anyone. It was as if we disappeared. There was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: There was no one there. There were in guards and you left quite easily. You advanced quite slowly. And you weren't even afraid.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, we were afraid, but we took the risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Why was there a risk?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you afraid of meeting someone, seeing someone on the way? Were you afraid because you said it was the road to Croatia? Were you afraid of meeting someone on the road on that route?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't think about anything at that point in time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How many people remained in that house after you left?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Quite a lot. Did they know you were leaving? Did you pack your things?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No. We just put our clothes on. We didn't take anything else with us. We just took the -- we just took clothes for the baby.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And then you left?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: And then we left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: We went to the Muslim part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How far is that? How long did it take you to get there on foot?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. We were almost running. I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But how far?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it took us 20 minutes or half an hour to get there. My sister-in-law said, "I can't go, continue," so we had to drag her there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to follow-up on some questions put to you by Ms. Nozica. With regard to the death of Plivcic Tahir and Softa, according to the information we have -- well, this information comes from Ivo. I'd like to know whether any investigations were launched into the death of these two individuals in order to find out who the perpetrators of the crime were, to find out how they had been killed. Was the father-in-law of Tahir, who seems to have survived the event, was he the person who referred the matter to the authorities to shed light on the event? That was my first question about the alleged killing of those two individuals. And my second question concerns the detention houses. You said that there were -- well, you said that your group had been split into two parts and that people were detained in two houses that belonged to the Kurbegovic brothers. And my question is: On what basis were the groups established? Did we have civilians, women and children on the one hand and members of the military on the other, or were these two groups established without following any specific criteria? I'd like to know why the HVO wanted to obtain information on the fact that one of their members had been killed according to your statement. This is also the purpose of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't no whether Tahir's father-in-law filed reports of any kind with regard to that event, but as far as the other part of your question is concerned, well, they put us in these two houses. I don't know whether it was really necessary. And the third question, I'm not sure that I understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase the first question. To date no official investigations were conducted in relation to the people killed in the village? Are you saying no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the next Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, madam. My name is Vesna Alaburic. I am a lawyer from Zagreb. I have several very brief questions I'd like to put to you on behalf of General Milivoj Petkovic, whom I represent in these proceedings. In your statement given to the Prosecution, item 11 of that statement, you said that the attack commenced in the night of the 12th and 13th of January, 1993, and today when asked by Judge Antonetti, you said that the attack took place on the 11th, 12th, 13th and January. Do you remember that? However, in item 11 you don't mention the day you say the Ustasha entered the village. Can you now tell us when members of the Croatian armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina entered your village?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. When you don't go out, you don't know what the date is. You don't know what the day is. You don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll now remind you of your statement given to the state security services on the 10th of February, 1994. You gave it in Bugojno. My colleague Senka Nozica showed you this statement. I think you still have it before you. It's to your right. Have a look at the third sentence in the statement which says as follows: "The Ustasha managed to enter Uzricje on the 18th of January, 1993, in the morning." Did you tell the state security services in Bugojno this? Is this what you stated precisely?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It's difficult for me to remember dates. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether some time had passed, a day or two, since the time when the village was shelled, as you said, and up until the time that Croatian soldiers entered the village?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I think we entered the dugout on the 11th or 12th, and I think we spent five days in the dugout, and then we got out when they came to fetch us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you were in the dugout for five days. That means that the -- what you said to be correct in 1994. Perhaps it was on the 18th that the Croats entered the village. And now -- my colleagues have said that the transcript hasn't recorded, something, so could you please answer quite clearly. Could you answer the question clearly. You said correct, in February, 1994, you told the State Security Service that the Croatian soldiers entered Uzricje on the 18th of January, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I'm interested in the word "succeed." When we use this word, it means someone made great attempts to do something and having made great efforts they succeeded in doing something. Is that what the word means in our own language?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So then can you explain the following for me: What did you mean when you said in 1994 that the Ustashas managed or succeeded in entering Uzricje? They made great efforts, they weren't successful, but finally they entered on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps it was the translator or the typist. I don't know, but they entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us or can you explain why the Croats were trying to take the village? Had they started shelling on the 11th of January but they couldn't get in until the 18th? So what was actually happening? Why did they get in so late? Was there fighting?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We were in the dugout. I didn't go out. We just heard the explosions, shells falling, until they came to fetch us, because you're underground. You don't go out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain something for us, because if you're in the dugout, well, you find yourself in one kind of situation and you can't see what's happening and as a result you can't see if any fighting is going on. What that the situation you were in?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You don't really know what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In other words, does this mean that it was possible there was ongoing fighting in your village but you weren't aware of the fact because you were in a dugout?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible. We were in the dugout, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just repeat your answer, because it hasn't been recorded completely in the transcript. My question was were -- was it possible that you didn't see the fighting in the village because you were in the dugout, and your answer was?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, we didn't see that. We were in the dugout. We knew about -- we didn't know about anything until they came to take us out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the family name Hasanic mean anything to you? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Let me think. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For example, the Hasanic family from Modric, does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, they were also refugees and they also looted these houses and took things out of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you describe this in greater detail? Who were they? Was the father Jusuf and the sons Elvir and Jesen and the mother and daughter in Nadina who were involved.

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were also involved in the looting until the fighting ended. They were also involved in the looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was this a Muslim or Croatian family?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I assume it was a Muslim family.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like you to explain the term it "Ustashas." Before the Croatian soldiers presented themselves as Ustasha to you on the 18th of January, how did you call Croatian soldiers in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I assume that you spoke about them. How -- what did you call them?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention them. I don't know what term I used. I know that they're -- ABiH and HVO were together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The HVO. So you knew that there was the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was the HVO often called Ustashas in the Muslim media?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There was no electricity, so we couldn't listen to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But before you arrived there, before the electricity supply was cut, had you heard such terms in the media?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you did know that the army of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina was called the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you saw such insignia?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in spite of this fact, why did you use the term Ustasha when you spoke to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I used the term that they used to present themselves with. It wasn't ill-intentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, I don't want to discuss whether this was convincing, whether soldiers presenting himself as an Ustasha is reliable but did you see insignia, HVO insignia?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: Well, no, they had no insignia when they came. None of them had insignia. Those in camouflage uniforms and those in black uniforms, they just said they were Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see any insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to clear up a small point. When the soldiers entered the village, how many weeks after that did you stay in that village, did you remain in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was at the end of February that I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the time you remained in the village, did the HVO soldier supervise the village? Did they guard you, or were you free to come and go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO did watch the village. We couldn't move around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And what did you do for food, to eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What reserves we had in the house we spent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was food to eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking this because looking at the Prosecution, because in paragraph 71 of the indictment, and -- it says, and I read: "It was winter, and every house had a wooden stove without electricity. Fifty to 60 Muslims detained in the houses received no food and stayed alive by eating whatever was left in these houses." Now you tell us, madam, that there was enough food. Were there small children, babies, with you and, if so, did you have milk for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This man had cows, so the children had milk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it right to say that during those few weeks everyone could eat normally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We weren't hungry, but we didn't really enjoy -- I don't know how to put it. We didn't enjoy ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another point which is also important: It was wintertime, the month of January, perhaps beginning of February. There was no electricity. The heating that you had with wood, you had wooden stoves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there a shortage of wood at some point or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had prepared themselves for the winter, the owners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to put a question to this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, while you were in that house, was any HVO member keeping guard in front of house or were they just passing by?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: They were guarding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were you free to fetch wood, to milk the cow?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: They were standing there when we went to the stable to milk the cow. As for the wood, it was inside. The people had already prepared enough wood for the winter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you receive any kind of food outside this house? Were you allowed to go to another house to get food?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know how to put it. A local man, he brought us medicines only.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I see. They brought you medicines. These guards in front of your house, did you have the feeling that they were there not to let you leave, or were they protecting you from some other persons that might harm you? Did you have any kind of unpleasantness when you were there?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No. I felt safe because I had nothing more to lose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But nobody hurt you in any way while you were in that house?

utterances.speaker: SENADA BASIC
utterances.text: No, nobody. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Any other Defence counsel? Mr. Ibrisimovic? No? So all Defence counsels have asked their questions. Has the Prosecution any additional examination or clarifications?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I have no questions in re-examination of this witness, but there are three short matters which I'd like to raise which do necessitate the presence of this witness in court during me raising these matters. The first is just to pick up on a point that Your Honour raised in relation to paragraph 71 of the indictment. It may be entirely my mistake, but I am not able to perceive the discrepancy that it appeared to me Your Honour was trying to point out in the indictment in that it states that Muslims detained in the houses received no food and stayed alive by eating whatever was left in these houses. And from what I've heard this witness say and indeed what is written in the statement, it appears that that is exactly what the witness is saying, that they stayed alive by eating what food was left in the houses, and I'm not sure, perhaps, I did not follow Your Honour's line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I could assist on that. I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I could assist on that, because the point is if they wanted these people to starve, they obviously could have taken the food away from them. That's the point. So there was plenty of food. And I think General -- General Praljak made an interesting point, and that was that you had guards there. So there is an alternative plausible explanation which is what the Rules call for when you have circumstantial evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not what I'm asking and I would appreciate the counsel not to draw inferences on my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm entitled to make my record and counsel should know better then to interrupt me while making my record. General Praljak was offering an alternative, plausible explanation as we are entitled to where there's circumstantial evidence and that is while they were guarded -- it's a two-way -- two-way sword. They're there for their protection -- to protect them from others. The food was available. They didn't starve to death and there's no evidence that any of the HVO soldiers or anybody went in to take the food away from them or prevented them from milking the cows. That's a pretty good indication that there was plenty of food and they were not being starved to death.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: With all due respect to my learned friend and not wishing to interrupt, my question was more directed at the Bench in case I had misunderstood something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. Madam Gillett, we're listening to you. I noted, Madam Gillett, that in the indictment there is reference to horrible conditions. So I was trying to check with the witness whether it was as horrible as that regarding the food and the heating. So you must know that whenever a Judge asks a question, we are being guided by the indictment and the legal qualifications of the crime, whether there was inhumane treatment, bad treatment, and so on. So that is why we asked this question. So if we have a witness who suffered such bad conditions, I wanted to specify what kind of difficulties they had regarding food and heating. Now, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The second point relates to a response I want to make to my learned friend, Mr. Murphy's objection to the tendering of Exhibit 7350. Just to pick up on what was mentioned in the objection, that whilst the witness, it is true to say, does not know the names that were in that document, the document does contain information other than a list of names, and it is about that that I asked the witness, and the Prosecution tendered this statement as corroboration for what the witness states in her statement and has stated here today in court, and that of course authenticity is only one part, relevance being the other, which I know the Chamber will take into consideration in considering whether to admit this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
